1.title: Principles in Context
1.text: Welcome to Module one: Principles in Context. It covers the exam area The prince two principles. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do seven things. one point one Analyze the application of the principles in context: ensure continued business justification. Learn from experience. Define roles, responsibilities and relationships. Manage by stages. Manage by exception. Focus on products. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: The prince two principles (ten percent). Exam format: an open-book scenario exam: one hundred fifty minutes, seventy marks, forty-two marks to pass. Validated against: the official prince two seven Practitioner syllabus (people cert), version seven point two.

1.title: How the exam tests the principles
1.text: How the exam tests the principles. The principles are the guiding obligations of the method. They are universal: a project that does not apply them is not using the method. The exam (Bloom four) gives you a behavior and asks you to analyze whether it applies a principle or neglects it.

1.title: How the exam tests the principles, continued
1.text: How the exam tests the principles. The figure shows this: The seven principles and the practices and processes where each one shows up.

1.title: How the exam tests the principles, continued
1.text: How the exam tests the principles. Use three moves: name the behavior, name the principle, judge whether the principle's purpose is met. Most principle questions hide inside practice and process questions, so this module is the lens for every later module.

1.title: The seven principles in practice
1.text: The seven principles in practice. Ensure continued business justification. In practice: A documented reason, checked at every decision, that can stop the project. Where it shows: Business case practice; directing a project; stage boundaries. Red flag: Case written once; project continues after the benefits are gone.

1.title: The seven principles in practice, continued
1.text: The seven principles in practice. Learn from experience. In practice: Seek lessons at the start, record them as you go, pass them on. Where it shows: Progress practice (lessons log); starting up; closing. Red flag: Same mistake repeats; lessons collected only at the end.

1.title: The seven principles in practice, continued
1.text: The seven principles in practice. Define roles, responsibilities and relationships. In practice: Business, user and supplier interests are represented and everyone knows who decides. Where it shows: Organization practice; directing a project. Red flag: Nobody can say who decides; an interest is missing; one person plans and assures.

1.title: The seven principles in practice, continued
1.text: The seven principles in practice. Manage by stages. In practice: Plan, monitor and control stage by stage; the board authorizes each stage; at least two management stages. Where it shows: Plans practice; managing a stage boundary. Red flag: One giant stage; detailed plans far ahead; no board decision between stages.

1.title: The seven principles in practice, continued
1.text: The seven principles in practice. Manage by exception. In practice: Authority is delegated within tolerances; only forecast breaches go up. Where it shows: Progress and issues practices; controlling a stage. Red flag: Board decides routine matters; a forecast breach is hidden. Focus on products. In practice: Agree what is delivered and its quality criteria before work starts. Where it shows: Plans and quality practices; managing product delivery. Red flag: A plan of activities only; nobody can say what "done" means.

1.title: The seven principles in practice, continued
1.text: The seven principles in practice. Tailor to suit the project. In practice: Adapt the method to the context and record it. Where it shows: Every practice; initiating a project (the P I D). Red flag: Method copied unchanged, or a practice dropped "because we are small".

1.title: The seven principles in practice, continued
1.text: The seven principles in practice. Two principles work as a pair: manage by stages gives the control points, and manage by exception sets the limits between them. Exam tip: Manage by exception does not mean "the board is never involved". The board still sets direction, authorizes each stage and decides when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded. It does not take routine decisions.

1.title: From symptom to principle
1.text: From symptom to principle. The board has not looked at the business case since the start. Ensure continued business justification. A supplier delay repeats what happened on the last project. Learn from experience. Two directors each believe they own the project, and no one has the users' authority. Define roles, responsibilities and relationships. Work nine months ahead is already planned task by task. Manage by stages. The project manager asks the board to approve a small purchase inside tolerance. Manage by exception.

1.title: From symptom to principle, continued
1.text: From symptom to principle. The project manager hides a forecast overrun until it happens. Manage by exception. The team cannot say what a finished permit form must do. Focus on products. The full method is applied unchanged to a two-week internal project. Tailor to suit the project. One symptom can touch two principles. Choose the one whose purpose matches most directly. Exam tip: Match the symptom to the principle's purpose, not to where it appeared. "Nobody agreed what finished means" is focus on products, even though it showed up at a stage end.

1.title: Tailoring: what may and may not change
1.text: Tailoring: what may and may not change. Detail and format of practices and processes. The principles themselves. Terminology, to suit the organization. The purpose of each practice and process. Number of stages beyond the minimum of two. A business case and board control. Roles combined, where independence remains. Independence of assurance from the project manager. Form and frequency of reports and meetings. Escalation when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded.

1.title: Tailoring: what may and may not change, continued
1.text: Tailoring: what may and may not change. Tailoring is driven by the context: size, complexity, importance, risk, delivery approach, number of parties, team capability, sustainability and digital and data needs. The project manager proposes it and it is recorded in the P I D, which the board approves. Effective: less effort without losing control. A small internal project uses a one-page business case, a small board, one stage after initiation and short reports. Not fit for purpose: a principle disappears: no business case, no stage approval, no product definition, no escalation route. Also a failure: the full method with long documents on a tiny project.

1.title: Tailoring: what may and may not change, continued
1.text: Tailoring: what may and may not change. Agile or hybrid delivery tailors the work inside a stage. Management stages, tolerances and board control remain. Exam tip: Tailoring changes how a principle is met, never whether. An option that drops a principle because the project is small, urgent or agile is wrong.

2.title: Judging a scenario about principles
2.text: Judging a scenario about principles. Find the behavior and who did it. Name the principle whose purpose it serves or breaks. Check form and purpose. A business case that nobody reads, or lessons that nobody uses, meet the form but not the purpose. Check tailoring. Would a lighter version still meet the purpose? Choose the reason that names the right principle and the real facts. Exam tip: If the board is asked to decide something the project manager can decide within tolerance, that is a red flag. The reverse is also a red flag: the project manager decides alone something that breaks a tolerance.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. In the build stage of Project Harbor, Sam Okafor asks the project board to approve a small software license purchase that is well inside the stage cost tolerance. Was this appropriate, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: No, because the purchase is inside tolerance and within his own authority. Manage by exception delegates decisions inside tolerance to the project manager, so taking a routine purchase to the board is a red flag.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Delta Software suggests that Sam Okafor write a task-level plan for the rollout stage of Project Harbor now, months before that stage starts. What should Sam do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Plan the next stage in detail and keep the rollout stage at a high level. Manage by stages keeps detailed planning to the near-term stage because distant detail goes stale, while the project plan still shows the whole project at a high level.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. At the end of the build stage of Project Harbor, costs are on budget but the benefit forecast is falling. Who should decide whether the project continues into the pilot stage? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: The project board, which authorizes each stage on the business case. Ensure continued business justification and manage by stages put the decision to continue with the board, not with the project manager, support or the delivery team.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Project Harbor's team records lessons only after the project closes, and nobody reviewed lessons from earlier Brightwater projects at the start. Which principle is the project neglecting? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Learn from experience, because lessons were not sought early or kept throughout. Learn from experience requires lessons to be sought at the start and recorded throughout, not collected at the end.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Sam Okafor proposes that a three-week internal Brightwater project should drop its business case, stages and board because the full method is too heavy. Was this appropriate, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: No, because tailoring changes how principles are met, not whether. The principles are universal, so a small project may use a light business case, a small board and few stages but may not drop them.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. At the end of the pilot stage of Project Harbor, forecast time savings have halved and sixty percent of the budget is spent. Sam recommends continuing so that the money spent is not wasted. Was this appropriate, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: No, because the decision must rest on the business case still holding. Ensure continued business justification means the decision rests on future value and not on money already spent.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Name the seven principles. Answer: Ensure continued business justification; learn from experience; define roles, responsibilities and relationships; manage by stages; manage by exception; focus on products; tailor to suit the project. Question two. What is the minimum number of management stages? Answer: Two: the initiation stage and at least one more. Question three. What does manage by exception use to delegate authority? Answer: Tolerances, with escalation when one is forecast to be exceeded.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Which principle is neglected if the board never rechecks the business case? Answer: Ensure continued business justification. Question five. What may be tailored, and what may not be dropped? Answer: The detail of practices and processes may be tailored; the principles may not be dropped. Question six. Where are tailoring decisions recorded? Answer: In the P I D.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Seven principles: continued business justification; learn from experience; roles, responsibilities and relationships; stages; exception; products; tailor. Exam skill: name the behavior, name the principle, judge purpose not just form. Stages: at least two; board authorizes each; detail only for the near term. Exception: tolerances delegate authority; forecast breaches go up. Products: agree what is delivered and its quality criteria before work starts. Tailoring: adapt how, never whether; record in the P I D; light is fine, missing is not.
